subtopic: RESOLUTION EXTENDING GREETINGS AND GOOD WISHES TO HIS MAJESTY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RESOLUTION EXTENDING GREETINGS AND GOOD WISHES TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to-day having been set apart as the day for the official celebration of the birthday of His Majesty the King, I feel sure that hon. members would welcome an opportunity to extend their greetings and good wishes to His Majesty in the form of a resolution of the House of Commons. I have prepared a resolution and have shown it to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), who has kindly consented to second it as worded. I would therefore move, seconded by Mr. Hanson: That, on this, the occasion of the official celebration in Canada of the birthday of His Majesty, King George VI, a humble address be sent to His Majesty in the following words:
"To the King's Most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
We, the members of the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled, desire respectfully to extend our loyal and heartfelt greetings to Your Majesty on this day set apart for the official celebration in Canada of Your Majesty's birthday.

At this time when, throughout the world, freedom itself is at stake. Your Majesty's calm courage, steadfast faith and active service have been an inspiration to your own peoples and to those of other nations joined in the common struggle.
It is our united prayer that, throughout these days of supreme trial, Divine Providence may continue to protect and guide Your Majesty, and that until the day of ultimate triumph and for many years thereafter, you may be given the strength to bear the great burdens which war has already created and may continue to impose.
With one voice we join to-day, as never before, in the words:
God save our gracious King,
Long live our noble King,
God save the King:
Send him victorious,
Happy and glorious,
Long to reign over us:
God save the King."
I would suggest that this resolution might be supported by the singing of the national anthem.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RESOLUTION EXTENDING GREETINGS AND GOOD WISHES TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext: I have the greatest possible pleasure in seconding the resolution, which I am sure will be carried unanimously with one single voice in this house, and will reecho from shore to shore in Canada from all loyal people of this country.

Motion agreed to.
Whereupon the members of the house rose and sang
God Save the King

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition) :
subtopic: REDUCTION IN VALUE OF RATION COUPONS IN MARITIME PROVINCES
speechtext:
In view of the gasoline situation in
the maritime provinces; in view of the number of questions on the order paper with regard to this matter; in view of the agitation which is still going on in those provinces, and especially in view of a statement issued by the premier of New Brunswick, a copy of which I sent to the Minister of Munitions and Supply this morning, is the minister in a position to make any statement that will allay the anxiety, if that is the proper term to use, of the people in that part of the country, and give them some reassurance that the so-called discrimination-that is not my term, but it is the expression used by friends of hon. gentlemen opposite-against the maritime provinces will be removed? Personally I think I understand the situation, but I should like the people of the maritime provinces to be convinced. They are not being reassured by certain persons both in New Brunswick and in Nova Scotia, and this ought to be done as soon as possible. I understand the old game down there, which is to stir up antipathy toward the central part of Canada, and it is not a creditable performance. I know that is a dangerous thing for me to say, coming from the province of New Brunswick. If the minister and the oil controller will give the people of eastern Canada a little more factual information, the maritime provinces will loyally accept the situation; but they have to be shown.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: REDUCTION IN VALUE OF RATION COUPONS IN MARITIME PROVINCES
speechtext:
My hon. friend will appreciate that I cannot state the stocks of fuel oil for the navy and air force; that certainly would be information of value to the enemy. I can say, in reference to gasoline, that the cracking at the Halifax refinery necessarily must be for the maximum recovery of: fuel oil. With regard to gasoline under the two-gallon ration, up to June 1 we actually slipped behind on our stock position; in other words we did not make or import as much gasoline
as was consumed under the two-gallon ration. However, the outlook for the future has improved considerably. We have been given some help in the matter of tankers by the maritime commission, and I can say that the situation certainly will not get worse and I believe will improve. Just as soon as the position warrants, of course we will increase the coupon value. As I have said many times, the purpose of coupon rationing is simply to distribute available supplies of gasoline fairly, and rationing will continue to be used for that purpose.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN VALUE OF RATION COUPONS IN MARITIME PROVINCES
speechtext:
Is the
minister able to give any indication as to when the full coupon value will be restored? An assurance on that point would be well received. While I am on my feet I should like to add something I intended to say previously. The whole position down there has been stirred up by one big dealer, who apparently found himself in possession of very large supplies of gasoline. He is stirring up all this agitation, and the minister knows to whom I refer.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: REDUCTION IN VALUE OF RATION COUPONS IN MARITIME PROVINCES

maintopic: ALASKA HIGHWAY-WAGES OF LABOUR IN YUKON- AGREEMENT WITH UNITED STATES AS TO WAGES AND WORKING CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the first question of the hon. member is yes. The national war labour board is at present considering placing someone in the Yukon district who will have charge of the enforcement of orders with respect to wages and working conditions there. I can assure my hon. friend that sympathetic consideration is being given to the suggestion he made in this house last Thursday.
It might be of interest to the house if I gave a summary of the arrangements that have been made between the United States and Canadian governments with respect to wages and working conditions, not only in the Yukon but in British Columbia and Alberta in connection with the building of the Alaska highway and other works that are being carried on.
By arrangement with the Department of External Affairs conferences were held with the representatives sent from Washington by the United States government with the object of agreeing on certain basic conditions.
The notes exchanged between the government of Canada and the government of the United States concerning the construction of a highway to Alaska provide that the United States government shall:
Arrange for the highway's completion under contracts made by the United States Public Roads administration and awarded with a view to insuring the execution of all contracts in the shortest possible time without regard to whether the contractors are Canadian or American.
In order to give effect to this agreement it has been arranged with the United States authorities that if contracts are let to United States contractors those contractors shall recruit their labour in the United States and shall not include persons normally resident in Canada. The labour so recruited will be paid at United States wage rates, which include a premium for work done abroad. The wages will be exempt, in accordance with the terms of the notes, from Canada taxation, and such matters as social insurance and workmen's compensation will be dealt with in accordance with United States law. United States rules as to working conditions will apply.
In the case of contracts awarded to Canadian contractors labour will be recruited exclusively in Canada. Canadian wage rates and working conditions will prevail. The wages will be subject to Canadian taxation;
unemployment insurance and workmen's compensation will be governed by Canadian law.
It is, of course, possible that in an emergency it may be necessary for United States contractors to engage some Canadian labour on the spot. It has been agreed that they will do so only through the Canadian employment service and that the labour so engaged will be paid at Canadian wage rates; that the wages will be subject to Canadian taxation and that Canadian law will govern unemployment insurance and workmen's compensation.
The reason for these arrangements is clear. The speedy completion of the road is necessary for the defence of Canada and of the United States. In order that the road may be completed as soon as possible, both United States labour and Canadian labour must be employed. United States labour can be recruited only if United States wages are paid and United States conditions of work apply. Consideration had to be given to our policy involving price and wage control, because it has been the practice in the United States to give extra pay for employment abroad. On the other hand, it is essential for the maintenance of the price and wage structure in Canada, which has been carefully devised to avoid the peril of inflation, that the wages paid to Canadian labour employed on the road should not be out of line with wages paid on other Canadian enterprises of a comparable character. By confining American contractors to recruitment of labour in the United States and Canadian contractors to the recruitment of labour in Canada, it is hoped to avoid the friction and the misunderstandings which are bound to arise if the same employer were employing two sets of men to do precisely similar work at different rates of pay. It is realized that this difference cannot be entirely eliminated, but it is hoped that a frank explanation of the circumstances will make it possible for the men concerned to understand what is being done and why it is being done, and to realize that the whole arrangement is designed to expedite the completion of the road without distorting the Canadian price and wage structure.
As a further precaution, United States employees are to be urged to assign a considerable part of their wages in the United States so that the cash payments which they receive in Canada will not, in most cases, exceed the cash payments received by Canadian labour.

It would be interesting to know the amount of the total funded debt of Canada held in the United States, and the annual cost (a) without exchange, and (b) with exchange. I should like to know, too, when the original debt was incurred. If I do not miss my guess it will be found that most of this indebtedness arose originally between 1922 and 1930. Those were the halcyon days when everything was going beautifully, and when New York was the mecca for all borrowers, particularly the treasury of Canada, and the provinces-not to speak of corporations in this country. I recall a certain warning given out in 1927, I believe it was, by a gentleman who then occupied this seat, against this kind of borrowing. No heed was paid to the warning we gave, and we are paying for it to-day, right through the nose. I hope this will be a salutary warning to all governments, no matter what their political complexion may be, that the debt of the country should be held within the country. If held in Canada no very appreciable difficulties will arise in handling it. It is the debt we owe to the stranger which may cause us great anxiety in days to come.
A short time ago I discussed this matter with a man who knows what he is talking about, and he told me that, taking the war and all other factors into consideration, the size of Canada's debt need not cause us much anxiety, so long as we owe it to ourselves. But when we go outside the country - to borrow we must be prepared for the worst, if the worst should come. That was sound reasoning. If we owe to ourselves we can take care of our debts by taxation, but we cannot tax foreigners. The man in

another country expects to be paid according to the terms of his contract. Attempts have been made to do that, but they have always met with tremendous reaction and resistance, and there have been reflections on the credit of the country. So long as we have this system we have to keep our conscience.
If the minister cannot give complete information to-day, he may do so at a later stage. I should like to have, in some detail, information as to the origin of the debt. I should like to have included the debt of the Canadian National Railways, because between 1924 and 1930 I believe this country borrowed on its credit in the New York market, through the medium of the Canadian National Railways, the sum of about $400,000,000. We are paying through the nose for that policy. I should like to know both the direct debt and the guaranteed obligations, so that the country will be apprised of the total burden upon which we have to pay principal, interest and exchange.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman wants
the particulars of the $459,000,000-when the debt was incurred?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Yes, when the first borrowing occurred.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
It will not be sufficient
merely to give the date of issue of the present bonds, because they may have been issued for the purpose of refunding previous bonds, and that procedure may have occurred two or three times. Does the hon. gentleman want similar information with regard to the Canadian National debt payable in the United States and guaranteed by the dominion government, and also the unguaranteed Canadian National debt?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Is that
in the form of certificates for rolling stock issued under the Philadelphia plan? There is a specific term that is used but I have just forgotten it. When I was on the railway committee in the old days we used to inquire about that. I thought they were all guaranteed by the government, although secured by a specific mortgage and subject to a trust.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
No, they are not guaranteed
by the government.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: The minister might include the obligations that are payable in New York, whether guaranteed or not.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: When an issue matures in New York and you arrange for a new loan to retire the old one, do you have to retire the old one in terms of the previous amount plus the exchange?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
If a loan is payable in
New York funds, so many dollars must be paid. We must obtain those New York dollars in some way.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
You do not get the
holders of the bonds to accept the new issue? I realize that that might not be possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: That is not the course followed.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I assume the new purchasers might not be the same as the old holders?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: The minister gave a figure of $459,000,000 as being the amount outstanding in the United States as at the end of April, 1942. Has he the figure as at the end of the previous fiscal year, so that we may see whether the picture has changed since the beginning of the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I have not the figures, but it has decreased $10,000,000 since the outbreak of the war.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Does that mean that $10,000,000 has been paid off in that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
More
would have been paid off if it had been considered the best thing to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: When bonds fall due, just what the government should do is considered carefully and arguments pro and con are weighed. I forget what maturity it was, but there was one where we finally decided that the best thing to do was to pay part and renew part.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Would it be possible to get a statement showing the total of Canadian securities, dominion, provincial, municipal and private, held abroad; also the dates of issue, the dates of maturity and the rates of interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I am informed that it
would be impossible to get that. The bureau of statistics makes an estimate, but as there is a certain movement in securities there is no way of finding that out with any exactness.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Could you not compel the owners of securities to register them by a certain date and thus get that information?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: The holders abroad?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I do not see how that could be enforced.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
There is one thing of which the hon. member can be certain. Holders of corporation securities, whether residing in the United States or in Canada, insist on being paid in New York funds when the securities are payable in New York funds. I have often wondered about the patriotism of those people. Perhaps I should withdraw that. If everybody were to give up his exchange it would be a wonderful
Third Victory Loan

thing, but one man will not do it unless everybody does. It is a terrible drain upon this country and upon the foreign exchange control board. I have been in that position myself. I am quite willing to give up to the state part of, shall I say, my unearned increment. If they want it all, they may have it so far as I am concerned.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Suppose the federal government desired to pay off its indebtedness in England and to call in all debts held in that country in the form of Canadian securities before making an additional gift of money; would it not be possible to find out what dominion, provincial, municipal and private securities were held there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
We have repatriated all
dominion government and Canadian National securities held by residents of the United Kingdom. The hon. member is probably referring to provincial, municipal and industrial securities.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: The United Kingdom government probably could obtain exact information with reference to the securities in the hands of residents of the United Kingdom by compelling a registration. They would have the authority to do that. However, that would have to be a programme carried out by cooperation between the dominion and United Kingdom governments.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Have there been any conversations with that end in view?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: No. Our programme did not involve the repatriation of industrial securities held by residents of the United Kingdom.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I am very much in favour of the billion dollar gift, but I do think attempts should be made to pay off whatever we owe in Great Britain, whether it is in the form of federal, provincial, municipal or industrial debts. In the long run it means that goods have to be shipped from this country to pay those government and private debts. I was just wondering whether we are going to get some of those securities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The matter was gone into pretty thoroughly in the debate on the billion dollar gift, and a good argument was advanced for not denuding residents of the United Kingdom of their Canadian securities. I do not want a repetition of the arguments advanced then, but so long as they have a substantial investment in this country they will have a financial interest in purchasing goods from this government and developing trade with us. If all these securities were brought home there

would be a strong tendency on their part to purchase wheat from the Argentine and cattle from other countries in whose properties and industries they had an interest.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I was reading through the debate the other day and it seems to me that that was the main argument advanced. An effort is being made to guarantee a foreign market for our products after the war, whereas we should try to develop our internal economy so that we will have a home market for our own products, or for the products for which our own products may be exchanged, rather than depend upon a favourable balance of trade. By this means an internal economy would be developed under which other countries could buy the production of Canada that was not required for our own consuming. You would be giving goods for goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I have always taken it for
granted that it would be impossible in the lifetime of any of us to develop an economy in Canada that would supply a market for the whole wheat production of Canada.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
But the goods for which
wheat could be exchanged.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
You mean goods such as
British goods?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Tropical goods.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Is not that argument
also applicable to the United States, that Canada might be wise to go there to a reasonable extent for the very reason the minister gives?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: That might be, but the question is not as acute with the United States as it is with Great Britain, because Great Britain purchases an enormous volume of goods from us, and the balance of trade is favourable to us as between Canada and Great Britain. All sorts of considerations come in there, questions of fairness, whether that is the right way to cooperate in carrying on a war, whether it is sensible from the point of view of postwar trade, and so forth. I realize that persons may have different opinions about it. This whole subject was pretty well threshed out in the debate on the billion dollar gift.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
When Canada negotiates
a new loan on the New York market to retire a loan, does the minister explore the possibility of raising a loan payable in Canadian funds rather than in United States funds?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I think that the floating of
a loan in New York payable in Canadian funds is impracticable. Some people in the

Third Victory Loan
United States used to accumulate Canadian bonds payable in Canadian funds, and they had reasons for doing so. But when you go into a market like the New York market to borrow money it is understood that you agree to repay the money they lend you, which is United States money.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: A few years ago some Canadian companies bought securities which were to be paid in New York funds. If I remember correctly, the city of Calgary had some legal troubles over an issue of that sort some years ago. Are any of the amounts in the list which the minister has given us payable in New York funds to Canadian companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: We do not know the holders or where they are. Some of these holders may be Canadians.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I can appreciate that there is the difficulty of obtaining foreign exchange in. the United States and that we desire to export gold for that purpose, but I understand that the great bulk of the gold we export to the United States is held in that country and therefore to that extent it does not in any way help the war effort of the United States and Canada taken together. To that extent it is an absolute loss so far as our combined war effort is concerned. I see that some of the gold mines are advertising in western Canada for men who are needed in other industries. The minister of munitions has told us that he could use right away five thousand mechanics at Arvida and a thousand miners at Sudbury. That makes six thousand men that he needs right way, and whom he could get if the gold mines in Canada ceased operating. The gold mines of. Canada are not making any real contribution to the joint war effort of the United States and Canada. Does not the minister feel that the production of gold could well be stopped for the duration of the war? After the war it would provide employment. We could have an agreement with the United States whereby the goods we require from her could be obtained under the lease-lend law, and then after the war we could repay our indebtedness to the United States in gold, if the United States desired to take gold. Our gold cannot be regarded as any help to the joint war effort of the United States and Canada. It is a help to Canada, but the war effort must be regarded as one joint effort by Canada and the United States, and the production of gold
does	not	help that	joint effort. On	the
contrary it is a complete loss of labour to the war effort.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Sooner or later the subject to which	the hon.	gentleman refers	willprobably come up for debate in some way. The hon. member has brought up this question	two	or three times before. He	hassuggested that we should close up the gold mines. He has asked me two or three times if I did not think that would be a very good idea,	and	I cannot	remember having	said
that I did. I should not like to express an opinion on it at the moment. I doubt whether this is the proper time to bring up the subject.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: The minister could at least say that the export of gold helps our foreign exchange.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Yes, if we are to go on buying from the United States and not be thrown into a relationship which is undesirable from our point of view, that of being a debtor, whether merely a debtor having obligations under the lease-lend law or otherwise. We ought to be in a position to pay for what we get. It makes for smooth delivery of goods, parts and materials to Canada, and gold is just what we need for that purpose. The hon. gentleman suggests that we should work out an entirely new arrangement, an arrangement which would be very hard on communities which rely on the production of gold, and very hard on the large number of persons employed in the industry. These social problems are of great importance, and these are all matters which would have to be taken into consideration if we were to adopt a policy such as the hon. gentleman has several times advocated.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: We already know of one community in the far north which is becoming entirely deserted. When the mines cease operation the business community that is dependent upon the mines has to fold its tent and move out, just as the miners do. They find another locality and start business, and the men must look for other employment.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
The minister mentioned the policy of lease-lend. This may not be the proper time or place to inquire with regard to that, but it would be interesting to know whether the policy is in operation, the extent to which it has been put into operation, the obligations that have been incurred both ways, and the balance for or against this

Third Victory Loan

country. If he could give that information it would be interesting. I do not assume he has it before him at the moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
We do not avail ourselves of lease-lend.
Mr.	HANSON	(York-Sunbury):	But	the
minister suggested	possibilities. It is definite
that we have not yet taken on anything under lease-lend?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
That is correct.
Mr.	HANSON	(York-Sunbury):	Has	the
offer been extended to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I always understood it was available to Canada if Canada wished it.
Mr.	HANSON	(York-Sunbury):	But	we
have not got it so far?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I am glad
to hear it.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I have been interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Acadia. I noticed in the evening paper that Mr. Little, speaking over the week-end, mentioned! that Canada was near an extreme labour shortage. In Saskatchewan the gold fields will become ghost towns, and while it is perfectly true that some of these towns were built up for the production of gold, they will suffer hardship if we discontinue production. The present may not be the time for the discussion of this important subject, but some minister of the crown should indicate whether any lead has been given by the government with a view to negotiation between the two governments to see whether the large number of men engaged exclusively in gold production and the amount of available equipment might not be used to better advantage. While there are hardships in moving people from a town in which they have been living for some years, there are greater hardships which they might have to contemplate. The point made by the hon. member for Acadia is well taken. We cannot afford at this stage to have highly trained men and valuable equipment producing goods that are not essential in the present conflict, and I cannot think of large quantities of gold as being produced in the best interests of Canada and the United States, taking everything into consideration. I wish the minister would indicate whether consideration might be given in the house to the whole question.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Would the minister also give us information regarding the action that is taken in Russia, Australia and South Africa? I understand that in Russia production has

been discontinued, and, to a large extent it has been discontinued also in Australia. H he could give that information it would be a lead on the question.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Ilsley thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 96, to authorize the raising, by way of loan, of certain sums of money for the public service.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: When shall the bill be read the second time?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I think it would be a good idea to read the bill a second time now. I should like to have a look at it. I believe the minister was to give me some information about foreign loans and guarantees. If I can get that information on Hansard, I am willing to have the bill go through. It is in the standard form of previous years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: I should like to look at it a moment. So far as I am concerned we could have the second reading and there would then be the committee stage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I move that the bill be now read the second time.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Mr. Hsley moves that I do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee on the said bill.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: In past years the second reading of a bill has been postponed just because the bill had not been printed in one of the official languages. Here we have absolutely nothing before us. There must be a stop to this.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: The bill has already been read the second time.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: When shall the house go into committee on the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR PUBLIC WORKS AND GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Next sitting.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The next order of business mentioned was the war risk insurance bill, but that presents new difficulties every day and I am not prepared to go on with it to-day. I am trying to work out with the Minister of Fisheries an arrangement which will meet the wishes expressed by some hon. members the other day; other questions have arisen as to whether the

Income and Corporation Tax
bill should apply to ships on inland waters or not, and certain information which is not in the possession of the government will have to be obtained. I cannot have that for two or three days, and it makes an awkward situation so far as this bill is concerned. I am proceeding to set up the organization just as if the bill had gone through, because I have to do it. I am getting committees together, and as soon as I have these preliminary matters settled, as far as they can be settled by the government, I shall have to bring this bill into the house again, but I cannot do so to-day or to-morrow.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I realize that the minister has
difficulties on his hands, but his colleague said distinctly that this would be among the orders of business to-day. Apparently there is no team-work between members of the administration with regard to these matters. However, I am not going to refer to that further. If the minister cannot go on and if there is a hope that he will be able to work out a solution for the fishermen, I would say we should let the bill stand over. As a matter of fact, all he has to do is to go into committee and then move the committee out; he has the remedy in his own hands. But I hope a solution will be found with respect to the fishermen.
He mentioned another difficulty with regard to shipping on inland waters. There was also a sharp division of opinion in the committee on another point which may occasion some debate here. So perhaps it is just as well to let the matter stand. But I want it understood that as far as we are concerned we were prepared to go on with the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We might revert to government notices of motion. There is a most urgent matter which my colleague the Minister of National Revenue would like to take up, the resolution standing in his name. speechtext:
Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve of the convention and protocol entered into at Washington on the 4th day of March, 1942, by the government of Canada and the government of the United States of America concerning rates of income tax upon non-resident individuals and corporations, the avoidance of double taxation, the prevention of fiscal evasion in the case of income tax and the exchange of certain fiscal information, and that this house do approve of the same.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bradette in the Chair.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES SIGNED AT WASHINGTON MARCH 4
speechtext:
This convention was signed on March 4. On the following day I made a statement in the house outlining the terms, or the chief terms, of the convention, and so probably it is not necessary to give a lengthy explanation to-day. It might, however, be advisable to give a brief review of the deductions at the source as between Canada and the United States as they have existed and been modified by a prior convention and as they are modified by the present convention.
In 1933, for the first time Canada imposed a 5 per cent tax deduction at the source in respect of dividends and certain interest leaving Canada. It was not until three years later that the United States first imposed a tax deduction at the source in respect of certain periodic payments made to persons resident outside of the United States. In 1936, when the United States imposed a 10 per cent tax deduction at the source it was felt that representations should be made to reduce that to 5 per cent so that there would be parity of deduction between the two countries with respect to these periodic payments. As a result, the convention of 1936 was entered into, and from that time until April 29, 1941, the deduction at the source of each country remained at 5 per cent.
In April, 1941, Canada raised its rate of tax deduction to 15 per cent, and in so doing automatically abrogated the existing convention. As a result, the then existing law in the United States pertaining to deduction at the source applied equally to Canada, as it did to all other parts of the world. The law of the United States required a deduction of 16i per cent, and thereafter 16J per cent was deducted in the United States.
However, the United States government then raised the tax deduction rate from 16i to 27i per cent, so that during the last three

This discrepancy in the amount of the deduction at the source again became the subject of negotiations with a view to parity of deduction. The negotiations culminated in the convention which has been tabled, and which was signed on March 4, 1942, by our minister at Washington, Mr. Leighton McCarthy, and the acting under-secretary of the treasury, Mr. Sumner Welles.
This convention, as my previous statement indicated, is wider than the prior convention of 1936. Broadly speaking, it does the following:
1.	It reduces the United States tax deduction at the source from 27i per cent to 15 per cent, and is retroactive, so that parity of deduction as between the two countries has been restored.

speechtext: From what date?

From April, 1941, the date when we abrogated the prior treaty.
2.	Certain extraterritorial features of the United States law as they impinged on the Canadian taxpayer are eliminated. By way of example, the United States law imposed a tax on any Canadian company, 50 per cent or more of the revenue of which was derived from sources within the United States, if the income was accumulated by a recipient Canadian company. Or again, if a Canadian company had 50 per cent of its revenue from the United States, then any Canadian indivdual resident who received dividends from that company was liable to taxation under the United States extraterritorial law. These extraterritorial features have been eliminated.

them?

Many of these claims antedated 1929. Many of our Canadian residents, if they did make some profits prior to 1929, suffered substantial losses thereafter, and I am informed, were called upon to pay their United States obligations; so that in the result, in some instances more money was paid into the United States than ever came out.

Representations were made to the United States government that such claims be not made, and for some time they were in fact not

made. However, after 1932 the United States revenue officials actively sought to Collect taxes in respect of these old transactions. These claims were resisted by Canadian taxpayers on the ground that they were not carrying on business in the United States, that they were not subject to the revenue laws of the United States, that they had been informed that the claims would not be made, and in fact they were not made for many years but were, as stated, subsequently revived. Now by the convention these claims are settled on the basis of the 1936 law as modified by the 1936 convention; that is, in general. 5 per cent in respect of any dividends or interest received from United States securities, and no claim in respect of any capital gains on stock market transactions. Any person in Canada who wishes to take advantage of this convention must, within two years from the date of this convention, apply to Washington for a settlement on the basis outlined. Therefore all persons concerned should take note of this requirement. Otherwise the law as formerly asserted by the United States might now be imposed as against those who fail to make such a settlement.

Under the terms of the convention the taxpayer who is liable under the earlier laws must file returns so that they will know he has made a disclosure of the interest he received during that period.
4.	If there is any case of double taxation arising by reason of a United States company doing business in Canada, or vice versa, and the company by reason of the apportionment of profits is being taxed on more than 100 per cent of its profits, it can ask for a conference between representatives of the two governments with a view to securing an adjustment.
5.	The convention also provides for an exchange of information pertaining to the payment of dividends, interest and other fixed periodic payments. This provision does not require Canada to give information respecting the income of residents of Canada.
6.	If the authorities of one of the contracting states are under the belief that the other country is being used as a basis of perpetrating fiscal fraud, a request for special information may be made pertaining to the activities of any such person, and after consultation the information may be exchanged. This is designed to preclude evasion and fiscal fraud.
There are other minor features in the convention which are self-explanatory on reading, and require no special mention at this time. This convention was ratified by the senate of the United States on the 28th day of May, 1942, and it only remains for parliament to pass this resolution. The convention, it will be observed, is beneficial to all Canadians who receive income from sources within the United States by way of interest, dividends, rentals, royalties, salary, and other periodic payments, by returning to them such deductions above the rate of 15 per cent as have been made from the moneys coming to them since April 29, 1941. It is also beneficial to the revenues of Canada, inasmuch as the tax deducted at the source in the United States is allowed as a deduction from the tax otherwise payable in Canada on the same income, and the smaller the amount deducted in the United States, the greater the tax payable in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the other night when I tried to speak on this measure I was ruled out of order. I do not know whether I shall be in order to-night or not. I see the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) smiling. I like to see him smile at me when I speak in this house because his smile is encouraging.
What I wanted to speak on was equality of service and equality of payment. We have a very difficult situation in Canada to-day with respect to clerical help. I do not say that each individual clerk in the house or each individual clerk in the country should not be paid what he or she is worth; but after all, we are trying to put a ceiling upon wages, and we are trying not to compete among each other for clerical help. Take, for instance, the girls who came to work in the civil service in Ottawa in the early stages of the war. Many of them came from patriotic motives and started in at a salary of approximately $70 a month. The next batch that came in got perhaps $90 a month, and the next batch, $120 a month or whatever it was. The result is that the large institutions in this country are finding it very difficult to keep their clerical help. I am not complaining about that. We will give our clerical help to the government if they need clerical help. But let us get together on a cooperative basis. As it is now, the government comes to the insurance companies, for example, the Sun Life, the Canada Life, the London Life, the the Dominion Life, the London Life, the Confederation Life, and so on, and says to them, "We need clerical help". I say: Do not come along and take our clerical help away from us, because the insurance companies are in this position, that we cannot pay our help any more than they are getting because their wages are frozen. What we have to do is to create new positions for these people. I suppose the various companies could get together and say, "We will trade you this crowd for that crowd, and we will adjust their wages." That is the only thing to do; but let the government come along to the insurance companies and say, "We need clerical help; what can you do for us?" That is what should be done instead of having the government go throughout the country taking this one and that one and raising wages. Moreover, it is an incentive to inflation. We will pay our clerical help the same as anyone else, but we should get together on a cooperative basis so that there
fMr. Ilsley.]
will not be chaos, because it will come to that unless we do something. We are all in the same boat.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What about the United States government? They are coming here, offering people $150 a month and taking them across.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Many young girls have gone from our institutions to Washington at $150 a month, but they have come back because the cost of living is so high that they are not as well off there as they are here. I think $70 a month is pretty low for a girl who is brought to Ottawa and has to get along in this city, with the rent and board she has to pay. I suggest that without very much trouble the government could get together with the institutions that are employing labour. Many people might take the view that life or casualty insurance is not essential to the war effort. I contend that it is essential in a sense. When one considers that a great many of the men who are overseas and others who are engaged in the war effort are protected by life insurance, it is an essential business. Not only that, but the life insurance companies have been the greatest source of our war loans. The companies collect money from the people and lend it to the government. I do not think we should have any more competition if we can avoid it. Let us get away from it. I do not begrudge these girls or men the wages they are getting, but unless we get rid of this competition I do not know where it will lead us. We shall have chaos. I should like to have an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will put in a word or two the point he wants answered, I will try to answer it. I understood from him that there was some movement of employees from one concern to another. Is that the problem?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The point is that the government is competing against essential industries or businesses for clerical help.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The salary rates in the civil service have been kept pretty well in line with what they have been in previous years. The classifications have not been changed. There has been a slight change with regard to those who have just come into the service or have been in for six months. The clerk grade 1, or stenographer grade 1, or typist grade 1, gets $65 after six months, and another grade was created, grade 1A, carrying a salary of $75, but that classification applied only to stenographers with two years' experience. These are not excessive salaries, and the only other concession the government has made to the changed situation, the great

War Appropriation
demand for labour, is the cost of living bonus to civil servants. That has been kept within carefully defined limits. I believe that in some localities where it is impossible to get clerks or stenographers without raising these salary rates somewhat, the rates have been raised; but if I remember correctly, they have not been raised beyond the maximum of the classes in any case, and I am surprised to hear that the government has been offering salaries that were excessive or greater than those paid by business. I do not think that is the situation. It might happen in a few individual cases, but as a general rule the government has not outbid business at all. Business is continually making offers to those employed in the government, and we are receiving representations to the effect that unless we raise salaries we shall lose our employees. The hon. gentleman may have seen the insurance companies' end of the problem, but I do not think he has seen the government's end of it. I do not think there has been any great bidding for help either by business or by the government. We have certainly tried to keep everything under control, so that there would not be.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There is one further point about this. The minister says there is no bidding. I could give him dozens of instances where girls with no experience whatever have been taken into the services, not through the civil service commission but in other parts-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Such as?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Does the hon. member mean enlisted girls?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I know they have been taken on. If we are to have a contented community, the government cannot take on a girl who has no more experience than an ordinary filing clerk and put her in a position where she gets $40 or $50 more than another girl who has experience. I am bringing this to the attention of the government because it is important that we get this down to brass tacks. If the government want girls or men let us get together with the government and let the government say, "We want so many from you and so many from you" and so on, and we will say to the government, "All right; you take these people; we will take them back after the war, but in the meantime we will try to train some more people for you." That is logical, but at present the situation is chaotic.

speechtext:
Would the Minister of Labour state the policy of the government with regard to work being done by the Japanese in the road camps?
This is the setting for my question. The minister will remember that after the California gold rush, the royal engineers sent a company round the Horn to what was then British Columbia, because it was feared that there might be rioting and insurrection among the gold miners who came up from the south. That rioting did not come to pass, and the royal engineers were put to work building roads. They built through that jungle country of the lower Fraser mainland; they built up the Cariboo and they started to build a road through the southern part of British Columbia from Hope in the' direction of Princeton. This was largely for the reason that gold was being discovered in all the creeks in that southern section. All this took place something like eighty years ago. Ever since then, attempts have been made from time to time, years apart, to make a join in that road between what was started on the east end and what was started on the west end of it. Now that the government's policy is to use certain Japanese males in road camps, certain camps have been erected and are being used at both ends of that gap, which is variously described as being from thirteen to twenty miles long. As far as I am aware, they have not reached the actual gap itself, but have been repairing and improving the roads approaching the gap.
The reason why I make these few introductory remarks is that all the people through the southern part of British Columbia as far as the Alberta boundary are looking forward with great hope once more to the prospect that that road may be finished, because it would considerably shorten the distance for all that traffic. When the Japanese first entered those camps at the east end of the gap, that is forty-three miles west of Princeton, the onlookers were disappointed to find that very little work was being done. There was no machineiy. They were afraid that once more they were going to look on at certain scratching of the earth without any result.
I am informed that a certain amount of improvement has taken place and that some road machinery has appeared on the spot. The minister of public works of British Columbia has all along taken a considerable interest in the matter and has stated that he has induced Ottawa to take rather a different view from that which Ottawa had taken of the value of that link from the point of view
War Appropriation

of defence. Whether that be so or not I do not know, but he has been endeavouring to put at the disposal of those camps certain pieces of road machinery. Unfortunately, however, all such machinery is in process of wearing out, and with the difficulties of getting more machinery the department of public works of the province does not want to see that machinery worn out too rapidly. Consequently, the people are once more becoming dispirited with regard to how the progress of the work will be kept up. So I ask the minister if he will be good enough to explain the policy of the government with regard to the Japanese in those camps, the facilities which will be provided for them to carry out the work, and the quantity and quality of the work which will be required of them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: First I would say we are going to press with vigour the road-building policy that is in operation at the present time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The building of roads. Second, there is a limit to the machinery available. In the next three or four months there will probably be going on in British Columbia more work of that kind that has for its purpose the successful prosecution of the war in that part of the dominion. However, it may be difficult to get the amount of road machinery we may require for these roads. My hon. friend can rest assured that all the machinery that can be got will be obtained.
With respect to the Japanese, personally I would rather see them employed for the relief of what one might call the acute labour shortage in certain other parts of the dominion; for instance, cultivation of sugar beets, cutting of pulpwood, and those lines of endeavour where there is an acute shortage of labour at the present time. But the slack will be taken up in these road camps. Take, for example, the transcontinental highway at Schreiber. I think that should be used as a reservoir for Japanese labour from which we can move them into pulpwood camps and sugar beet fields in western Ontario, as we are doing at the moment.
I am well acquainted with the district of which the hon. member speaks, and from my point of view I should like to see that road completed because of the quicker access it would give between the section to the east thereof and Vancouver.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It would be a valuable addition to the road communication in the west. It was pointed out by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruiekshank) on more

than one occasion that the road and two railways are located very close together in the Fraser canyon, and that sabotage might produce an unpleasant situation there. This at least would be an alternative and additional road. Is there machinery available from any other source than borrowing from British Columbia?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not know. The general machinery situation is difficult right across the dominion. That must be admitted. While we have some machinery that belongs to the Department of Mines and Resources, the procurement of other machinery at this time is not easy, particularly in view of the work on the Alaska highway. However, the hon. member may rest assured that whatever machinery we can get will be obtained in order to complete the road to which the hon. member refers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
When this
bill was in the resolution stage the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) made an exhaustive statement in regard to the increased consumption of liquor in Canada. Nothing has been said by anyone on the treasury benches as to government policy in that regard. I do not propose to-night to go fully into the cogent arguments so well advanced by the hon. member for Mackenzie; it is hardly necessary to do so. He pointed out then that the increase in liquor consumption in Canada during the past year has been alarming. In one province that increase was as high as 35 per cent in 1941, as compared with 1940. Bodies of Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific have become somewhat concerned about the matter. The wartime prices and trade board, which operates under the Minister of Finance, has had to call upon the people of Canada to accept rationing of sugar, tea, coffee and many other commodities in daily use; yet here is a traffic which requires sugar, honey, cereal grains, equipment, labour and so on, the use of which is bound to take away from Canada's war effort at least to some extent. The Minister of Munitions and Supply tells us constantly of the difficulties in regard to shipping; yet, as the hon. member for Mackenzie pointed out, one firm alone in Canada exported 400,000 cases of beer.
This is a difficult thing for the people of Canada to understand. It has often been stated that the reason why more military equipment was not available at Hong Kong and the Malay peninsula was lack of shipping space; yet Mr. Philip Guest, British United Press correspondent in the far east, in his reports from the scene of conflict made the

War Appropriation
statement that before Hong Kong was captured 600,000 bottles of whisky were destroyed, and that before Singapore fell 800.000 bottles of whisky were destroyed. Apparently shipping space had been found at some time or another for the shipment of supplies of this kind into what were potential danger zones. It is difficult for the people of Canada, who are being called upon to make sacrifices; for the children of Canada, who are being asked to do with less candy and sugar, to understand why there should be a privileged group who so far seem to have been completely excluded from the necessity of accepting any sort of rationing. Even now, when one goes into a restaurant and orders milk, he gets a glass of milk instead of a bottle, because the glass is no longer available for bottles of milk in certain circumstances. There appears to be no suggestion, however, of rationing the glass that is used for the bottles necessary for the liquor industry. When I was in western Canada a short time ago I noticed in one of our newspapers an advertisement inserted by the breweries, suggesting that people should buy a bottle of whisky and give the bottle to the Red Cross. They did not suggest to whom the whisky should be given.
I think the government ought to make some statement on this matter. I am not suggesting now that advantage should be taken of the war in order to try to introduce prohibition. That is not the question at issue at all. The point is that here we have a lucrative trade, which has grown by leaps and bounds during the period of the war and which so far has not been made subject to any form of restriction whatever, as far as we are aware; which is using materials, labour, machinery, shipping space and all the rest of it, while other commodities which are required by the great majority of the Canadian people, and some of which are essential to the welfare of the people, are being rationed and curtailed.
It seems to me that before this debate concludes, we ought to have some statement from the government, particularly from the Minister of Finance, under whom the wartime prices and trade board operates, as to just what is the government's policy. Does it propose to allow this traffic to continue, in spite of the fact that other commodities are rationed, or has it some policy with reference to the brewing and distilling interests in Canada? I wish that at some time during the debate the minister would give us such a statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I was hoping that we might finish this bill to-night. I am not prepared to make a statement on the
question raised by the hon. gentleman. As he was speaking I was wondering why he was bringing up this subject under this section. Apparently he is arguing that because there is some rationing of commodities such as tea, coffee, sugar and so on, which have to be transported long distances over water, therefore a commodity which is manufactured in Canada and of which there is no shortage- perhaps there should be a shortage of it, but there is not-should also be rationed.
I have received quite a number of letters from persons who argue in the same way, and a great many of their arguments are extremely unfair. For instance, there is the argument that the government could find space to send beer to Libya but could not find space to send equipment to Hong Kong. That argument is going the rounds in certain circles; it has an interesting sound and is being rather widely circulated. As far as finding space to send equipment to Hong Kong is concerned, of course we did find space to send equipment there.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Too little, too late.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Well, we had every reason to think the' equipment would reach there in time, but unfortunately, because of certain developments, it did not. Reference has been made to beer being sent to Libya. The beer in that instance was purchased by a British government agency, not by the Canadian government at all, and the British government found space for it. As I understand the situation, there is not a shortage of space in ships going in one direction.
The same argument is used with regard to whisky coming here from England; the same thing is said about that. We did not have anything to do with arranging for the shipment of beer to Libya; that was a matter looked after by the British government. I suppose they thought it would be a good idea to get some beer to the soldiers in Libya; and while I know my statement will not meet with universal approval, I think the attitude of a great many people who think it is a crime to send beer to soldiers in Libya is wholly reprehensible. When one considers what the forces of the empire are going through in Libya, a tropical country where it is very hard to get the right kind of water, or any water; when one considers the deaths that men die who are taking part in tank warfare, I think a good many persons here in Canada who are making sarcastic remarks about the sending of beer to soldiers in Libya could be better employed.

War Appropriation
As far as the regulation of the sale of liquor is concerned, no one comes out and says we should have national prohibition. I did not hear the remarks of the hon. member for Mackenzie the other night, but I do not think he advocated national prohibition, nor do I think anyone in any province is advocating provincial prohibition. Hon. members know that if we were to begin to interfere with the hours and conditions of sale, we would be up against certain problems. They know, too, that there is a different problem in every province. They know there is public sentiment in one province for one kind of regulation, and public sentiment in another province supporting another kind of regulation. After tremendous difficulties, tremendous heartburnings, and troubles of every kind, we finally, in this dominion, got the control of liquor on a basis of regulation by provinces, and by provincial governments, and we are going to leave it there-as long as we possibly can, anyway-because if the provinces cannot assume and discharge the responsibility of regulating the sale of liquor, then they are incapable of taking that share in the war effort which I think they are capable of taking.
I presume the reason why the provinces are not more rigid in their regulations respecting the sale of liquor is that they find that public sentiment in those provinces is not in favour of it. The point I do not understand is why persons are converging their attack on the dominion government when, in fact, the provincial governments have the responsibility. I do not know whether provincial governments wish to assume that responsibility-but I think they do. That is where those persons who are advocating a more rigid curtailment of the sale of liquor should go.
When we come to the matter of rationing I would point out that liquor is not comparable with commodities concerning which there are shortages. With regard to the use of Canada's resources-well, some grain is used, add I suppose there is some machine capacity. Practically all of it is now in those plants. It is very much limited in its use of labour, and is in an entirely different position from the manufacture of refrigerators, automobiles or other manufactured articles which directly take steel and other commodities from our war effort.
I do not say that the sale of liquor should not be curtailed. I do not say that the government should not do anything in that direction. But let us put it on the correct ground, the ground that the consumption of a large quantity of liquor by the people of the nation is bad for the nation. Do not get it on the specious ground that we should treat the sale of liquor the same as we do tea, or

the same as we do coffee, or the same as we do sugar. That is a specious ground, and it is not sound reasoning. Do not put it on a ground of that kind; and do not put it on the ground that it is taking steel, machinery and one thing or another away from the war effort, because in fact it does not take nearly as much away from the war effort as a great many other things which hon. members would not argue should be stopped at all.
I am not talking in favour of the liquor interests. A favourite tune played is that the government is under the control of the distillers and brewers, and that we are repaying some kind of debt, or something like that. I do not know anything about any debt to the distillers or brewers. Their interests are the last which concern me-or concern the government, so far as I know. I do not believe that those are considerations at all; I know they are not considerations which govern.
It is a common thing to pick up a letter which says, "You have taxed everything else, but you have not taxed liquor." As a matter of fact, at the beginning of the war the duly on spirits was four dollars a gallon, and now it is seven dollars a gallon, an increase of 75 per cent. At the beginning of the war the tax on malt was six cents a pound, and it is now twelve cents, representing an increase of 100 per cent. At the beginning of the war the tax on wine was fifteen cents a gallon, and it is now forty cents, or an increase of more than 100 per cent. A charge frequently made, and about which I have patiently to write a denial, is that we have kept our hands off the liquor people, and that we have not imposed taxes on them at all. A year ago, when the budget was being prepared, I looked into the matter respecting the consumption of spirits and I found that the consumption of spirits had risen very little in 1940 over 1939. It will be remembered that the budget was brought down in the spring of 1941. I found that the consumption of beer had risen about 20 per cent, I believe it was, in 1940 over 1939, and we increased the tax on malt from ten cents to twelve cents a pound. What it will be possible or necessary to do in the future I do not know; and certainly I am in no position to make any statement to-night on the matter.
I would advise hon. members who are directing their attention to this matter to address themselves to the provinces, whose prime responsibility it is to regulate and control the liquor traffic.

My point is that when the federal government believes curtailment of the sale of any product is in the interests of Canada's war effort, the fact that the commodity comes within provincial jurisdiction is not permitted to interfere. The minister cannot shelve the responsibility simply by saying that this is a provincial matter. This is a federal matter, in view of the fact that this country is at war. If it is in the interests of Canada's war effort to take this step, the federal government ought to take it. Then he proceeded to build up a straw man and to knock him down again, by referring to what people have said about sending beer to Libya. I was not talking about sending beer to Libya.
