speechtext:
I have not taken any part in this debate which has lasted for some six weeks. I had determined that I would not because I thought I could best serve the country by keeping quiet and letting the session come to an end in order that the government might go on with the war work. I also had some feeling of sympathy for the tired, overworked, half-dozen members of the government who had to bear the brunt of the attack that has been made upon them. At first I thought this was a good thing because the attacks that were made were circulated through the press, and then the ministers rose in their places and explained the whole thing away, showed that what had been said was absolutely untrue or capable of suitable explanation. I thought that was the best business at the time.

But conditions are changing. As hon. members all know, I do not speak in this house for any one but the people I represent. That is to say, I speak for no party, either as the leader of it or as a member. But I do speak for the people I represent and have done so for many years. I know what they are saying; I know what they are feeling; I know what they are doing, and I know what they are hoping. I know that this all sums up to a profound dissatisfaction with the conduct of the government. No doubt in many instances this feeling is unjustified, but that is the consensus. This applies also in some measure to the opposite side of the house. The feeling in Comox-Albemi is, "for God's sake, quit talking and get on and do something."
The bickering and the talking that went on in connection with the plebiscite, the delay in taking the necessary action, incensed the people. Still they sat and they listened and they looked. When the plebiscite passed in a most decided manner they expected quick and prompt action. But they have not got it. If any country, if any body of men expected that something would happen this week, it was that Bill No. 80, to amend the mobilization act, would be brought down either to-day or to-morrow. We now find that that is not to be done because of what appears to be a misinterpretation on our part of. the Prime Minister's statement. But I think we were led into it. We understood that this bill would be brought on when the appropriation resolution went through the committee. However, we are now confronted with the explanation that what was said was with reference to the passage of the complete bill, perhaps weeks hence. There was a profound disappointment among hon. members here, and I am sure there will also be profound disappointment throughout the country.
The people are demanding action now, and nothing else will suffice. This feeling is being concentrated in ill will toward the government or toward the leader of the government. But it is spreading also to a feeling of general contempt for constitutional government. The people are asking, "What are those fellows in Ottawa doing? They have done nothing for six months; they are leaving us in the lurch when we want action." This feeling is perhaps stronger in British Columbia because of our greater expectation of enemy action. I leave that thought with the government. Speaking for the people whom I represent, I urge the government to bring on Bill No. 80 and a bold, forward-looking policy at once.
As it has been mentioned to-night, I should like to say a few words about the Japanese situation. A number of these people have been moved, much less quickly than we

War Appropriation
expected and hoped, to areas outside of the so-called restricted area, which is along the coast. But they have been located in such a way and in such a manner that the people are justifiably incensed and alarmed. I understand the idea has been to put the women in some of the ghost towns. That is all right, provided there is a guard around them. However, the able-bodied men are being put in road-building camps. Generally these roads are located along the railroad because the railroad naturally chose the best route, and the road is bound to follow. I am not blaming the government for this, but several camps have been set up in British Columbia, with two or three hundred Japanese in each. My information, which I consider is most reliable, is that these three hundred Japanese are provided with picks and saws and axes. An axe can be a very dangerous weapon if one wants so to use it. To guard these men there are three white men, each with a rifle.
If you had three guards in the penitentiary, one of them located on a balcony such as we have here, if anyone down below moved he could threaten to shoot. If he did shoot he would bring the whole penitentiary guard to his assistance. But at these camps it is simply Tom, Bill and Harry who are doing the guarding. It is true that each man has a rifle, but there is nothing to hinder the Japanese from crowding around and asking what time it is or if he would give a match. Then when the guard is surrounded a Jap could stick a knife in him. If the guards are working in three shifts, the other two men would be sleeping. If they are not working in three shifts, then things are worse; the three men would go to bed at night and leave the Japanese to do anything they liked.
It may be said that these camps are located where they could not do much harm, but wait until the right moment comes and it will be too late. I have tried to find out-but so far I have not been able to get any information- but I understand that no check is made of express parcels being sent to these Japanese. These parcels might contain dynamite or anything like that. Most of these camps are within short distances of the railroad. There is one camp in particular within a quarter of a mile of two railroads and a bridge. If one particular bridge were put out of business, the whole traffic to eastern Canada would be cut off. A Japanese with a few sticks of dynamite which had been shipped in to him by express could go down and blow up that bridge, and British Columbia would be cut off absolutely from the east. It may be said, "Oh, well, they would let us know and we would get people to them," but how would we know? The
Japanese would overawe the white men and sweep down the valley taking everything in front of them.
There is another feature. The bridges are supposed to be guarded, but that is being done in the same sort of happy-go-lucky fashion. You know, Mr. Chairman, we are at war with a bitter and brutal enemy, and a vital bridge should be properly guarded. We kept a guard outside this building last summer. Air force men did guard in front of this parliament building. That was a spectacular thing, and it was all right. But guarding a bridge in war time is different. A man may be walking up and down a railway bridge, and it may be 150 feet down to the water. All that would be needed would be for someone to pick him off with a rifle, and that would be the end of him. Then his assailant could easily blow up the bridge or touch off a charge of dynamite and destroy a vital connection. This is war, real, bloody war, and we must have an effective guarding of vital bridges.
The people out there are getting all wrought up, and naturally so, and if you had a wife or daughter of the teen-age in those districts you would be concerned too. Do not have any illusions that the enemy will adhere to the rules of the Geneva convention or anything of that kind. Get that out of your head entirely, and at least make this attempt to meet the situation. Have these camps connected by telephone. Possibly they are now. If not, it could be done very easily, and there should be a telephone system connecting the men who are guarding the bridges with some central office. Of course, the blowing-up of a little culvert would not do very much harm, but a vital bridge is a different matter, and any money spent to protect these bridges would not amount to anything like what it would cost us if the bridge were destroyed. Have all the important bridges connected by telephone, and have the guards telephone to the central office-it does not matter where it may be-at fixed hours. Then, if a guard does not telephone in at the appointed hour, say eleven o'clock, you would know there was something wrong, and you could get hold of a ranger unit and ship them out to that spot. That is the way we do things in war. If the guard did not telephone from the camp or bridge at eleven o'clock or one o'clock, or whatever hours were agreed upon, the central office would know that the man had been attacked or murdered and that it would be necessary to stop the trains and turn out the troops. The expense would be a mere bagatelle, and it certainly would relieve people's minds, the wives and mothers of men who are fighting overseas for us to-day. It is their women and children whom we must
War Appropriation

protect. It is up to us to be especially careful, and we are not being especially careful. We are having these vital spots guarded in a perfunctory fashion, like turning out a guard of honour for the lieutenant-governor. What we want is to do it as it should be done in war time. In India, where there used to be occasional raids from the hills, we had double sentries, one man marching east and another west, so that everything was always in plain view of one or the other. Let us do this thing in real war fashion and really protect these vital connections, as they are not being protected to-day.

Mr. Chairman, what remarks I have to make on Bill No. 95 I can make on paragraph (a) of section 2, which reads:
2. (a) the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada.
I presume that the vote of $5,500,000, under the heading of surveys and engineering branch, in the statement put on Hansard by the minister at page 2922, giving details of the war appropriation for 1942-43, pertains to a roadway from Prince Rupert to Terrace and to Cedarvale. I have been wondering whether this vote goes far enough. I do not think it does. I am for this road, for the purpose is to build a roadway from Prince Rupert to Cedarvale, a distance of about one hundred miles. The route from Prince Rupert to Cedarvale continues on to Hazelton and to Vanderhoof, and thence down to Prince George in north central British Columbia. After the roadway from Prince Rupert to Prince George is complete, if connecting links east were also completed, it would be part of a connection with the Alaska highway; but it ends nowhere, as far as the Alaska highway is concerned, even if it is completed from Prince Rupert to Cedarvale, Hazelton, Vanderhoof and Prince George. Whoever is in charge of the engineering plans covered by this vote should suggest a further appropriation to enable this roadway to connect central British Columbia and east of the mountains.
The Alaska highway runs from Fort St. John northerly to Dease, and thence to White Horse. All that is intended to be done under this vote is to build a road from Prince Rupert to Cedarvale. What is gained is a through road from Vancouver to Prince Rupert-all very necessary and something with which I am in hearty accord. But it does not go far enough to give a connection with the Alaska highway. Whoever authorized the plans could have gone further and submitted plans for a roadway from Vanderhoof via Fort St. James to Manson Creek, and thence through the mountains to Finlay 
Forks, the source of the Peace river. From Manson Creek there is no connection east. A large part of the road from Vanderhoof to Manson Creek is largely passable, perhaps by motor cars. If the hon. member for Cariboo were here, he could tell us whether the roadway is passable for cars. It is only another thirty-five miles from Manson Creek to Finlay Forks; from there east, if the roadway is carried on to Hudson Hope and Fort St. John, is a distance of approximately one hundred and twenty miles, and at Fort St. John the road would connect with the Alaska highway.
To deal with this project as this vote does, is dealing with a very important connection in a piecemeal fashion. If the government intends by this vote to accomplish a real defence, where does Alaska and Yukon defence come in under these plans, when there is no connection with the road east of the mountains and the Alaska highway, which is being built by the United States government from Fort St. John to White Horse, and then on to Alaska? I cannot understand why this vote did not go further and really get us somewhere as far as the defence of the Yukon country is concerned. The vote should have been for twice this amount, and the road should be carried through the mountains to Fort St. John to connect with the Alaska highway. There is no road from Fort St. John east. The road is completed from Peace River to Hines Creek, but from Hines Creek to Fort St. John it is not completed.
While I support this vote, I want to impress on the minister that the vote is not sufficient, and the road should go farther to connect with the Alaska highway. I see the Minister of Labour nodding his head, and he is right in nodding his head. This road does not connect up with the Alaska highway, and therefore I should like the minister to get in contact with the engineers and suggest to them that they ask for another appropriation to connect this Prince Rupert roadway at Vanderhoof with one through the mountains as outlined in the plans and specifications that accompany this vote, to Hudson Hope and Fort St. John. In that way we would have a real defence road.

The peculiar thing about
this debate is -that we go from alcoholic beverages to Japanese and then to roads. I wanted to say a few words before the hon. member for Comox-Alberni rose, but he was a little ahead of me. I wished to refer to two matters mentioned after he had spoken, the question of alcoholic beverages and the Japanese. In the minds of some people the first is the more vicious of the two; to my mind the second is the more vicious.
On several occasions in the last two or three weeks we have heard a great deal of criticism from members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation with regard to the stand of the government on the question of curtailing the sale of alcoholic beverages. I think it is time that parties who question the government on certain policies should have a policy of their own. The question arises to-day, is the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in favour of the curtailment of alcoholic beverages? If they are, let them say so. But what they say is, "Where does the government stand? What is the government going to do about it?" You cannot debate a question by evasions and questions. I am not so sure that we are not allowing to rise in this country the same old arguments we had in the last war, which resulted, after the war, in conditions of which none of us were very proud and which eventually every province in Canada but one repudiated. If members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believe there should be curtailment of the sale of beer, wine and alcoholic beverages of all kinds, let them move an amendment to have that done. If they think that space is being used in ocean carriers to carry beer to the men in Libya, and that it should not be done, let them say so. These things cannot be done by innuendo. Most hon. members recall the campaign in the last war in every province of this dominion, the committee of one hundred in Toronto, committees that were organized in other provinces. I well remember a little skit that appeared in the papers at that time, written by a man who had spent three years in the trenches in France. As I recall the words it ran something like this:
I read of these tea and coffee blighters Who rave about kingdom come.
They want to stop our cigarettes,
They want to stop our rum.
Water, they say, would be better.
Water! Great Scot! out here We are up to our necks in water,
Do they think we are standing in beer?

I remember that, and I remember the agitation for the curtailment of beer and rum to the soldiers, closing the canteens throughout all the allied nations, and then the agitation to stop cigarettes. How far would these prohibitionists go? If the time has come that we are going to talk about the curtailment of alcoholic beverages and all these things that appear to be vices in the eyes of some people or some parties in this house, let hon. members come out and take a clear stand, put themselves on record so that it is known where every member of this house stands, instead of trying to throw the responsibility on someone else by innuendo and to gain a certain amount of kudos without taking any stand themselves. It is time we took a stand on this question.

labour conditions in the shipbuilding industry of the province of Quebec, an inquiry should be made into matters pertinent to these demands in the three firms above-mentioned and in any other firms that may be designated by the Minister of Labour.
The minister accordingly recommends that a commission be appointed, under the provisions of part 1 of the Inquiries Act. . . .
Then it states who are to be members of the commission.
The minister also recommends that the commissioners have the right to determine the manner of conducting the proceedings in respect to such inquiry and to make all necessary inquiries and investigation for the purpose of ascertaining what w-age or other labour conditions should be established and whether or not such conditions should be uniform in the plants under inquiry, the commissioners to present their report on the matters investigated and their findings and recommendations to the Minister of Labour; in making their recommendations the commissioners to have full regard to the wartime wages policy prescribed in order in council P.C. 7440, dated December 16, 1940, as amended by order in council P.C. 4643, dated June 27, 1941.
The minister further recommends that all fees and expenses payable to the commissioners or to witnesses or other persons w-ho may, under their authority, be concerned in the proceedings of the commission. . . .
Then follows the usual provision found in these orders in council. As I have already mentioned, this commission made a very full report, appended to which was a schedule of wages covering all the shipbuilding plants of Ontario and Quebec. I might add that a further order in council was passed giving the commission authority to investigate the shipbuilding plants of the province of Ontario, as well as those of the province of Quebec. On January 26, 1942, order in council P.C. 629 was passed, reading as follows:
Whereas the Minister of Labour reports that a plan for the stabilization of basic wage rates in certain shipyards has been developed on the basis of the recommendations of the royal commission on shipbuilding in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, the reports of certain boards of conciliation and investigation under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act and various submissions from employers and employees concerned;
And whereas the minister further reports that in the interests of industrial peace it is desirable that immediate effect should be given to the aforesaid plan;
Now, therefore, his excellency the governor general in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour and under the authority of the War Measures Act (chapter 206, revised statutes of Canada, 1927), is pleased to order and doth hereby order as follows,-
1.	The basic wage rates for mechanics and the cost of living bonus for all employees in the shipyards, specified in the statement attached hereto, shall be adjusted as of the dates and in the amounts indicated in each case;
War Appropriation

2.	The Minister of Labour is hereby authorized to adjust the basic wage rates for other classifications of employees of the aforesaid shipyards in such relationship to the basic wage rates specified for mechanics and in such amounts as in his opinion, have regard to all the circumstances, are fair and reasonable.
That order, in my opinion, puts into the hands of the Minister of Labour the power to decide what are fair and reasonable wage rates. I have before me the wage rates recommended by the royal commission for the various classifications, as well as those in the schedule attached to order in council P.C. 629. In the Kingston, Collingwood and Midland shipyards the royal commission recommended basic wage rates of eighty cents for mechanics. In the Kingston, Collingwood and Midland shipyards the order in council lays down a basic wage rate of seventy-five cents an hour. In the case of the other shipyards concerned the same differential exists; there is very little difference. There is a difference in the wage rates of Marine Industries Limited, where the scale recommended by the royal commission was seventy-two cents and sixty-seven cents, while under the order in council the basic wage rate established for mechanics was seventy cents.

speechtext:
If this is an Irishman's fight, I will get into it. I am prompted to rise this evening because of a question I asked the Minister of Labour this afternoon, with respect to the marketing of coal in Nova Scotia. The answers I received from him and from the Minister of Munitions and Supply were anything but satisfactory. In view of the fact that the Minister of Labour, as chairman of the national war labour board, took upon himself by means of an order in council the functions of negotiator between the unions and the employers, I am going to go into this situation a little more fully to-night. I think the whole matter has been badly handled. First, there has been a lack of a national fuel policy and, second, the negotiations carried on by the national war labour board with the miners have not been of the best.
Almost two years ago I brought up in the house the marketing of Nova Scotia coal and the necessity of that fuel as an essential war commodity. I pointed out to the Minister of Munitions and Supply that the time was coming when ships would not be available for the transportation of coal up the St. Lawrence and

that the facilities on Cape Breton island for the shipment of coal to the mainland needed considerable improvement. The strait of Canso is a bottle-neck that should have been remedied some fifty years ago. The assembling yards needed considerable extension two years ago, but nothing has been done. I have written the Minister of Munitions and Supply on two or three occasions to ask if something could not be done to improve the shipping facilities across this strait in order to accelerate the transportation of coal and other necessary war materials-there are a lot of them being produced on the island-but his last communication was to the effect that because of the large expenditures being made it was not considered economical to make this expenditure at this time. The strait is only a mile wide, and it could be bridged or tunnelled. Much money has been spent in Canada in the extension of plants and so forth which were not as badly needed as is improved transportation along this particular line.
There is no excuse for the coal situation that exists in Canada at the present time after three years of war. The fuel controller broadcast that fuel would be rationed, and the Minister of Munitions and Supply stresses the fact that those using oil for domestic purposes will have to use some other fuel. The fuel board is perhaps doing the best it can as a strictly administrative body, but it is subject to orders from the department of government under which it functions. It administers regulations only, and I do not think there is sufficient latitude in the regulations to enable it to do the job it should be doing.
There is no excuse for the mines in Nova Scotia working on a three day a week basis. A short-sighted policy has placed us in the position where we have no other transportation facilities available. From time to time we eulogize our relationship with the United States. There is a market in the eastern states for Nova Scotia coal, and there is a market in central Canada to Quebec for Pennsylvania coal. Surely this situation that has now developed must have been seen months ago. I cannot understand why the fuel control board or the minister or someone else who had access to the facts and was in a position to judge the road ahead could not have arrived at some understanding whereby coal could have been marketed in the places I mentioned. Nova Scotia coal could be marketed in the New England states right into the Boston market and United States coal could be shipped by rail to Ontario and Quebec. This arrangement could last for the duration of the war. It should have been done, but it has not been done.

War Appropriation
I am led to believe from discussion with at least one of the officials of the fuel control board that they have some plan in mind. We are, however, facing a serious situation at the present time as far as fuel is concerned. I should like to amplify the statement I made that the minister and his department through the national war labour board have usurped the normal bargaining powers of the trade union movement and that as such they must accept the whole responsibility for the negotiations that are carried on. They have taken over the functions of a union dealing with an employer. Orders in council 7440 and 8253 have definitely wedded the unions to the national war labour board instead of to the employer. Unfortunately, since that has taken place, the experience of the miners' unions in Nova Scotia has not been very happy. They had their difficulties in the past with the operators, but their difficulties have been considerably increased since they started to deal with the national war labour board. There has never been a contract signed with any degree of satisfaction since the government took over that function.
In 1940, the McTague board, appointed under order in council 7440, made certain awards. While they were not all they should be, those awards have never been lived up to. The McTague board recognized the fact that miners' wages in Nova Scotia were 7-1 per cent below the 1926-29 levels, and in accordance with the terms of reference set out in the order in council those wages should have been increased, but during the negotiations the company proved to somebody's satisfaction that they did not have the money. They have been broke ever since they came into Nova Scotia. The award made by the McTague board was a cost-of-living bonus of thirty cents a day. The board set out in their report that the company could not pay the thirty cents at that time, but that they would pay fifteen cents a day and that as their financial condition improved, the additional fifteen cents would be paid. One of the arguments which the mine-workers' union are having with the war labour board now is that the company should be forced to live up to the award made by the McTague board in 1940. The miners have been patient and long suffering, but the company now takes the position that they do not have to pay that additional fifteen cents and that they are not going to pay it.
Just a few weeks ago the miners' union presented a brief here which sets out their case clearly. I am not going to read it. No
doubt the minister is familiar with it. What I am saying now is said from memory with reference to the McTague board award. The company owes the miners of Nova Scotia, if the McTague award means anything, a bonus of fifteen cents a day retroactive to February, 1940.
As I understand order in council P.C. 8253, the national war labour board is given no power to determine wages or bonuses based upon a company's ability to pay. It is a straight matter of fixing a cost-of-living bonus in keeping with the index as laid down by the government. That is my interpretation of the order in council. But when the miners' union met the national war labour board, the board took the position, after an examination of the books of the company by some auditors-

speechtext:

miners and the operators.

speechtext:
That is right. They asked
for an impartial examination of the affairs of Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation and its subsidiaries and the ability of that entire organization to pay the rates asked for by the miners of Nova Scotia. The auditors made a partial examination of the coal industry, but make no mistake about this, you cannot examine coal without examining steel because they are interlocked. There were timber lands, wire-nail companies, and so forth -altogether twenty-six subsidiaries owned and controlled across Canada by the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, and so I say that the analysis made of the company's books was only a partial one and certainly does not give a true picture of the affairs of the company. On the surface the figures presented to the national war labour board might indicate that the company had no money, but I would call the minister's attention to what is said by a standard authority on Canadian and international affairs, a booklet called "Trend," issued on April 17, 1942, from 231 Jesse James-or St. James street, Montreal, and in it I find this observation on the financial page, "Splendid progress of Dominion Steel and Coal". This was in April. They go on to say:
The management of this corporation was sufficiently far-sighted to rebuild and improve plants and properties very extensively before the war.

speechtext:
You would not object
to that, would you?
War Appropriation

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Not at all, but wait until I come to their financial position, and remember, the company maintain they are broke. It goes on:
The result of this policy has been that more than $20,000,000 has been ploughed back into the business, from earnings, since 1935. Thus Dominion Steel and Coal is well equipped to take a prominent part in Canada's war effort.
The point I make there for the benefit of the chairman of the national war labour board and the Minister of Labour is this, that you cannot examine coal in Nova Scotia without examining steel and the other twenty-six subsidiaries of this corporation. Where did they make their improvements? Did they plough back any of this $20,000,000 into coal, or did it go into industrial plants in some other part of Canada, and was it charged back to their coal operations? Is that why they are broke? That angle was not probed at all. Only coal was probed, and the decision of the board was based! on figures presented by the company that they were not able to pay. If the company has ploughed back $20,000,000 it certainly did not go into the coal industry, and yet it might have been produced by the coal industry. That is something which the minister should endeavour to find out. This controversy over wages will never be satisfactorily settled until somebody is big enough to examine the financial structure of this whole organization.
I quote still further from this standard authority on Canadian and international affairs:
What this means to shareholders-there are 1,039,083 shares of no par value outstanding- is revealed by the following salient points:
1. In past five years-1937 to 1941 inclusive . . .
Do not forget that they were broke in 1941 and could not pay 15 cents a day bonus. It goes on:
1.	In past five years-1937 to 1941 inclusive- net profits have averaged $1,241,000 or $1.24 a share.
2.	During the same period, working capital has improved by over $7,000,000, to the current figure of $13,349,317. This is equivalent to approximately $13 a share.
3.	Earned surplus amounted to $6,028,059, or nearly $6 a share.
That picture certainly does not coincide with the figures presented to the national war labour board by the auditors who made the examination and said that the company was not in a position at that time to bring the wages paid in Nova Scotia up to the 1926-29 levels as required by the order in council. So much for that controversy with respect to wages.
(Mr. Mitchell.]
I understand that the door is still open, that the mine workers' union are still negotiating with the minister, and I am merely jogging his memory on this question of the company being broke and unable to pay. I should like to know where that $20,000,000 went and where it came from. Was it ploughed back into industrial plants in Ontario and Quebec? Did any of it go back into coal? Again, if this earned surplus of $6,028,059 was earned in the five years including 1941, certainly the company could not have been as poor in 1940-41 as they made out to the McTague board and the national war labour board. I expect that the mine workers' union will be meeting with the board again, and I would ask the minister to consider whether under order in council P.C. 8253 the board have authority to determine wages and bonus on the basis of the company's ability to pay. As I read the order in council, they have not that power. They may interpret it differently. That point certainly needs clarification.
There is another point I would bring to the minister's attention, and I am doing this, not for the purpose of criticizing but because I want to be helpful and to avoid friction. I know the miners of Nova Scotia have contributed their full share in the war effort. They led the province in the last war loan. They are making the full contribution they are permitted to make to the armed forces. They are not allowed to enlist. You would get many recruits from these Nova Scotia mines if you would let the men join the army. They are a class of people who have been badly abused. Only last summer they were black-guarded over this dominion in full-page ads which stigmatized them as saboteurs, sabotaging the industry, when they were accused of sitting down on the job. But I am absolutely certain that other factors were involved there.
In the face of the situation facing us to-day, these mines are working only three days a week. There was a full-page ad in the Halifax Herald of April 8, 1942-I have it here, and it must have cost a lot of money-put out by the Dominion Coal company to try to prove to the public, to the government and to anyone who was ignorant of the facts that the miners of Nova Scotia were curtailing production by absenteeism and all that kind of thing.
That was in April, 1942, and here they are, a few weeks later, with 50 per cent less time being worked. There are no full-page advertisements as to the reason. They met the

War Appropriation
miners' executive board and all they told them was, "From now on we shall be on short time", but the reasons are not made known. The people of Nova Scotia and the public of Canada are not children, and they are not going to take very kindly being treated as such. If there is a reason for curtailing production in the fuel industry and people have to tighten their belts and make sacrifices, then the cards should be laid on the table face up, and the people should know about the situation. If you can tell them that lack of shipping facilities is responsible, very well; they will take their share of the sacrifices that are necessary. But they want to be told.
In the past two or three days I have received dozens of telegrams asking me to find out from the government why mines should be working half time. What is the reason? The people there say they can get no information. Talking the matter over with some officials who have to do with the movement of coal, I find they take the attitude that either the company, or the government, or somebody in the know, should make a statement. There is no reason why the people should not be told.
With respect to the steel industry there is another thing which is militating against progress. This is a national industry which is necessary for the war effort, and instead of its being set up as a national industry under the jurisdiction of the national war labour board, who have the steel controller in Ottawa and are in possession of all the facts and figures with regard to wages and so on pertaining to steel, and where difficulties could be ironed out expeditiously with the heads of the union, the position is taken that steel is a secondary organization, and regional boards are set up across the country. In each province there is a regional board, and steel comes under these boards. These boards are dealing with matters in connection with which there are great difficulties in getting the facts. The thing should be coordinated. It is a national industry, and it should be taken under the wing of the national war labour board.
To show how silly these regulations are, or how silly somebody is who lays them down, let me mention this. Steel, a national industry, is handled by regional boards; but when we come to a little isolated salt mine in one corner of Nova Scotia, making application to the regional board for an adjustment of grievances at Malagash, the minister of labour of the province, or one of his officials, advises these people that salt mining is a national industry and comes under the national war labour board. One lone little salt mine has
to come to Ottawa for redress, but a great national industry stretching across the country and essential to the war effort has to be taken apart piecemeal in the different provinces, with considerable loss of time, confusion and friction. I suggest to the minister that he should consider bringing that organization under the national war labour board.
Another thing I would express my opposition to is the manner in which the cost of living bonus has been handled. Bad as it is, it was some compensation to workers in the war industries. Under order in council P.C. 7440 they were given something to compensate them for the rise in the cost of living, and at least they held their own. They were not worse off than when the war broke out, as far as the basic rates were concerned, and in the war industries wages are to some extent higher than in the non-essential industries. Take truck drivers, clerks for your department stores, and so on-a large group of people making up a considerable percentage of the wage-earners of Canada. Their wages have always been very low. They received no cost of living bonus, and many of them have received absolutely nothing in the basic rates. When order in council P.C. 8253 was passed there was a proviso in it that led these workers to believe that they were being brought in and were to be given the equivalent of a cost of living bonus, equal to what the workers in war industries were receiving. Then there was a lot of happiness on their part. But after P.C. 8253 was passed, another order was passed that added a clause which completely wiped out any benefits that might accrue to the workers in the categories I have mentioned.

in under the original order, P.C. 601, I believe. In Canada the cost of living has affected practically everyone, and it seems to me that everyone in the country should be treated on the same basis. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Those receiving bond interest?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If the income is sufficiently low, I would have no hesitation in saying that. If someone has an income of $1,000 or $600 in that group, received from bond interest, that person should certainly get the cost of living bonus. There should be no discrimination on that basis if that is all they take in. I have no hesitation in making that statement.
There is another matter in regard to which I would ask the Minister of Labour to tell me something. I wish he would interest himself in it. I have tried the Minister of Munitions and Supply for the last eighteen months but have not been successful. He has been very nice about it and I am not going to quarrel with him, but I have received no satisfaction. There is a machine-shop in Glace Bay. It is owned by the Dominion Coal company and employes from 300 to 400 mechanics, trained, skilled men as good as will be found in the country. In the last war that shop was engaged in producing war machinery, turning out bomb casings for one thing. It has not been utilized for that purpose in this war. The other day I made representations to the minister, pointing out that it is working on short time. The men are prohibited from taking employment in any other essential industries unless they are released. They requested, and I requested the Minister of Munitions and Supply, if it were possible, that he look into the shop and find out what use could be made of it. I made that request a considerable time ago. 
The minister wrote stating that an inspector was being sent for the purpose, but I never received the report. A few days ago I wrote again, and the minister said he would have the inspector go and see what could be done. At the present time the minister, or his department, is trying to adjust the grievances of the men on slack time, who are also petitioning for a release from that plant so that if they cannot be used there, they can go to another.

drift from one part of the country to another and take employment where they can get it, the registration will not be much good.

I certainly would. It would be in the national interest. I want the minister to take under consideration the possibility of using these men somewhere else, or using that plant. It is well equipped and is certainly not doing much war work, no work which could not be replaced very easily, the repair of cars and some locomotive repairs. There is a large body of men there, well trained, who could take their place in war industry anywhere in Canada.
I am sorry to have occupied so much time. There is much more I could say, but I will reserve it for another time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I will endeavour to cover most of the points mentioned by my hon. friend in his informative remarks. Of course he will appreciate that with the vast amount of work being done by the national war labour board and the regional boards it is impossible to carry in one's head all the details of the complicated negotiations beween the Nova Scotia miners and employers. I would say, however, that both the miners and operators requested that the books of the firm be gone into by an independent firm of chartered accountants. I do not know of any objection being raised by either side to the firm selected, McDonald, Currie and Co., of Montreal, one of the outstanding firms of chartered accountants in the dominion. Frankly, what they found was that there was no money in the till. My hon. friend has read from another publication. It might be the advertising medium of some bond house. It must be clearly understood that nothing I would say about coal miners would be anything but to their credit, because the men who go into the bowels of the earth have a hard job. Very few people would care to undertake it, although miners get it in their blood, and men who come from the old country drift into the mines again even when there is opportunity to get employment elsewhere. I am not saying that their wages are high enough, but they are the highest ever paid in the history of the industry, and the full cost of living bonus is being paid. There are twro exceptions, two subsidiaries where there is some back pay coming. That was made possible by an increase in the price of coal to the consumer.
That is the picture as we saw it. I have no brief for the kind of advertisements issued by the company. I think they are unnecessary under present conditions. The most important thing in Nova Scotia is, to my mind, to get the negotiations based on what I think is the only basis on which trade union negotiations can be successful; that is, on character and good faith on both sides. If the national war labour board has done anything to assist in that direction, I believe its institution has been well worth while.
My hon. friend knows of the trials and tribulations that have existed between employers and employees in the coal mines of Nova Scotia. He can rest assured that if in my small way I can assist in having negotiations carried on in a more friendly manner than in the past, I will do everything I can.
I was very much impressed with his suggestion as to the possibility of shipping some of this coal to the United States. If my hon. friend had the information that the government has, he would see the difficulties, matters over which we have absolutely no control, due to lack of certain transportation that existed in past years. We hope that difficulty will pass away, but at the moment it is a problem that neither I, nor he if he were in my place, could overcome.
The hon. member also brought up the question of steel being a national employer under the national war labour board. I played some part in drafting the order in council and the regulations that set this, what I consider a courageous policy, in motion. We had to decide what would be national organizations and what would be'regional organizations. We came to the conclusion that certain dominant trades or callings that in years prior to the outbreak of the war had come within the jurisdiction of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act were probably about as much as the national board could handle. I feel that after the war the provinces will demand their constitutional rights and prerogatives, and wages and hours of labour being generally understood to be within the jurisdiction of the provinces, we considered that it was much better to let the provinces work in their own field rather than that the federal government should invade it. I might say also that the attitude adopted by the provinces, their willingness without exception to cooperate, is an exemplification of the will of the Canadian people to give every aid possible to the successful prosecution of the war and the formulation and undertaking of such policies as we think necessary in that regard.
Might I also pay tribute to the employees' organizations as well as the employers'
War Appropriation

organizations? I never thought I would live to see the day when the three dominant labour organizations of this country would even sit down together in a room, let alone sit round a table and carry out the arduous duties arising out of decisions on applications from labour organizations and employers' organizations in connection with the very difficult problem of wage negotiation. I may add this, that up to date the national and regional boards have rendered decisions in over five thousand cases; and I think this should be said in favour of the employers, for goodness knows they are hammered enough, that, strange to say, the great majority of the applications have come from employers who want to increase the wages of their employees.
May I add this, incidentally. I believe that on the basis of trial and error we can fashion, through the instrumentality of the national and regional boards, a wage policy which will reflect credit on our good sense and lay the basis of what one might term a permanent institution of wage negotiation in this dominion. I might say also-and I think history will judge us in this regard-that the launching of the price and wage policy of the federal government was the most courageous legislative act on the home front in the history of this or any other democratic country. Let us not forget that we can lose a war by inflation just as easily as we can lose it through lack of equipment with which to fight the war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: What would bring it about?

speechtext: Certainly they are, and that is why I am going to make this point. It would be no great trick for my organization, when the cost of living began to rise, to go to the employers and say, "Stand and deliver."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is that the cabinet?

speechtext: No; it is the engineers. This policy treats everybody alike. It treats the lowest paid and the highest paid worker in the same way. I think that is equality of treatment, based on the fundamental practice which we regard as one of the corner-stones of our civilization; that is, that you cannot have different laws for the rich and the poor dealing with the same subject. I think it can be fairly said that some people are inclined to be disappointed if a policy works. I believe this policy is working on all six cylinders to-day. During the same period in the last war the cost of living increased by something over 12 per cent. Since last October the cost of living has increased by -4 per cent, which in effect is an increase of 12 per cent in the purchasing value of real money.

And the
poorly paid man received no compensation.

That is what I want
to develop. I want to be very frank about this. I would not support this if I did not think it was going to benefit the chap who cannot help himself. That was why the policy appealed to me. Take the people on old age

pensions, the people receiving mothers' allowances, the men and women receiving workmen's compensation benefits, the dependents of soldiers, sailors and airmen, the soldiers, sailors and airmen themselves, and that great class in the country who live on fixed incomes-I am not talking about incomes in the higher brackets-those people who are almost defenceless when there is an increase in the cost of living index. I sincerely believe that through this policy we have maintained the morale of those people at a level which did not exist in the last war.

On the basis of the
minister's reasoning, should these people not be entitled to the cost of living bonus that industrial workers are paid, at the initial stages?

the order, but not mandatory.

But the government
has not implemented it.

speechtext: Oh, absolutely.

I agree with that, but
the hon. member will see the force of my argument, and he will appreciate the effect on the morale of the people. I have a very clear recollection of that; and even the most powerful trade unions on the north American continent never caught up with the cost of living. I think it is far better to stabilize conditions, as we are trying to do, than to permit a condition similar to that which existed during the last war. After all is said and done, if you see a thing in operation it is much more vivid than any idea you get from reading a book. I have a very clear recollection of some of the conditions created in Germany after the last war by the inflationary movement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: I was speaking about the steel industry-and I do not know what my hon. friend should take exception to. I had said that if you take the steel industry away from the regional boards in Nova Scotia-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I will tell you, when you have finished, what you do not know about it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
When you take away the steel industry you are taking away a big percentage of the industry of Nova Scotia. There may be some point in what the hon. member has said with respect to salt, and that steel is as much a national industry as is salt. That may be true.
In so far as steel and coal are concerned, I was always led to believe that coal did carry steel. That was the story in Nova Scotia many years ago. But we must all realize that the steel industry was a hard industry to start in this country. Years ago this government bonused steel, to a great extent. I think the people of Cape Breton felt that with the natural resources of coal they would build up a secondary industry with steel, and the reason they could build it up was that they had the coal.
I am not for one moment saying a word in defence of the corporations in charge of steel and coal in Nova Scotia. I had to deal with their problems many years ago when I was in the Nova Scotia legislature. Many changes were made from time to time, and it may be that the repairs they say they are putting on their plants, to show a loss, are the result of present-day auditing methods which have become so important and so specialized in these days. At the same time the hon. member's remarks relate to the regional boards in Nova Scotia. I believe both steel and coal are represented. With a local knowledge of conditions and with men on it who represent the industry, I believe the miners of Nova Scotia will get a better deal from their own people than they would from the outside.
I cannot think of anything else the hon. gentleman said in so far as Nova Scotia is concerned with which I cannot agree. He was rather reasonable in his presentation. He has spoken from the point of view of those he represents, and it is commendable that he should do so. At the same time there are economic problems that do not always appear on the surface, and it seems to me that before a discussion of this sort goes out to the public we should be careful that the thing is analysed in an intelligent way that is representative of the true idea of what the people want.

speechtext:
It is no surprise to me, after listening to the hon. gentleman, to find * out
exactly why Nova Scotia ends at Halifax. It is also not surprising that everything east of Halifax is back about fifty years in comparison with the rest of Canada. The hon. member makes the observation that he has heard this question of bridging the strait of Canso raised in this house for a number of years. I raised it two years ago, and it would be very handy to-day as a war measure. I think the hon. gentleman either misunderstood what I said or has attempted deliberately to put another construction on my words. He seldom speaks in the house until someone else bases an argument for him. I notice he is touchy when one begins to analyse Dominion Iron and Steel and Coal. Perhaps he is closer to them than I am.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No; I am not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: When he sets himself up as their defender with respect to the marketing of coal in the United States I say that he deliberately misconstrued what I said.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The hon. member cannot say that I deliberately misconstrued what he said. I did not intend to misconstrue anything.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Withdraw.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is the matter? Withdraw what?

speakeroldname: The ACTING CHAIRMAN (Mr. Ross, Calgary East):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The hon. member should withdraw his charge that' the hon. member deliberately misconstrued his remarks.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I will withdraw. When the hon. member tries to ring in the question of subventions, which he knows is a touchy one in Nova Scotia, he does it for political purposes. I did not mention subventions in any way, shape or form. I realize that the fuel situation in Canada was an emergency, but apparently he does not. When I suggested the transfer of markets I did so in order to facilitate Canada's war effort. I was not thinking in terms of after the war or profits for corporations or subventions or anything along those lines. Some of my hon. friends who preach a good-neighbour policy seem to have very little faith in that policy. They say that we may not be able to do this after the war; that we may not be able to do that after the war. If we do not get busy and do something about the war, we shall not have anything to say about what we shall or shall not do when the war is over.
I mentioned the transfer of markets as something that would take care of what I considered was an emergency fuel situation.

War Appropriation

I have no criticism to make of the audit that was made except to say that one cannot examine Dominion Iron and Steel and Coal and determine the wages of coal by simply making a partial examination of the coal end.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I might say to my hon. friend-and this is not said in any spirit of criticism-that there was no objection by the miners. They did not raise the contention he has raised. They asked for the audit, and there was general agreement that the company that was employed was a fair company. The thought the hon. gentleman has brought into the discussion was never raised before the national war labour board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The workers representatives are far from satisfied with the decision of the board. The argument I am making to-night is my own, based upon my knowledge of the situation. My criticism of the audit was not that the auditors were incompetent-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The minister implied it. My criticism was not that they did not do the job they were sent to do. I simply observed that one cannot determine the ability of the Dominion Coal Company to pay without considering their twenty-six subsidiary organizations across the country. They can transfer capital from one to the other; they can plough back money from coal into steel, into wire nails, into timberlands, into railroads and shipping or into anything else that they control and show it as operating costs against coal. If you do not probe coal and steel and consider their relationship to the subsidiary organizations, you do not get a true picture of the financial standing.
I think it is a small job for a member from Nova Scotia to sit down with his pencil and attempt to pick flaws in anything I may have said with reference to the interests of the province. Dominion Iron and Steel and Coal has a large staff of experts who are quite capable of taking care of their interests without that kind of cooperation from a member from Nova Scotia. I do not care where a member sits in this house or to what party he belongs; if he is advocating something in the interests of Canada, I am with him.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Does the hon. member not believe in free discussion? I was most courteous to him and simply pointed out that the subventions had enabled us to get coal into these markets. I suggested that if we wanted to get United States coal into this country, all we needed to do was to take off the subvention.
I said that I did not think the people of Nova Scotia wanted the subventions taken off.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The hon. member fails to recognize the fact that the mines in Nova Scotia are working only three days a week.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Take away the subvention and how many will they work?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The hon. member has not the slightest idea of what he is talking about. You are subsidizing United States coal right now into those two markets and you are rationing your fuel.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
